title: Oankar close
hookLine: a poem made of a scholar's own alphabet, sung back to him as an invitation: closing the Oankar with humble learning

lines: THE ONE WHO REMEMBERS NOT KNOWING.
NOT WHAT IT KNOWS. HOW IT TEACHES.
cards: Often not the one who knows the most, but the one who remembers what it was like not to know: the patient older cousin, the coworker who says, I got this wrong for years, here's what finally helped.

For a week this path has read the Oankar, Guru Nanak's long alphabet poem, spoken to a pandit, a teacher of letters. Today we close it, and the question isn't what the poem knows. It's how it teaches.

teach.b: First, look back. The poem opens with Oankar, the One, from whom even Brahma came. It asks whether the pandit has understood what he reads.
It stands on a riverbank where a tree can fall at any time. It says true learning is reflection on the Name, and that a record is being written. Second, notice who it's spoken to.
Its center line, the Rahao, says, in paraphrase: listen, pandit, why write about the world's tangles? Write the Name of the Lord, as one who faces the Guru. Listen.
It doesn't mock the teacher or tell him to burn his books. It leaves the letters on his board and asks them to carry the Name. That's an invitation, not a defeat.
Third, look at how Guru Nanak speaks of himself.
In the Japji, after a long list of the world's foolishness and cruelty, he signs the stanza, in paraphrase: lowly Nanak offers this reflection.
The one bringing a new reading of the alphabet doesn't stand above the learner. He sits beside him and calls himself small. Fourth, put the two together.
The Oankar teaches humility to the learned, and it teaches humbly.
Knowledge that looks down on people has missed the poem's point. Knowledge that kneels beside someone and says, here, look at this letter with me, has caught it.

how: The Oankar is sung in kirtan and explained in katha, where a teacher goes through Gurbani line by line, seated before the Guru Granth Sahib.

o: a final verdict against the pandit's books
a poem that teaches the learned, humbly
the closing prayer said after every hymn

games.q: closing the Oankar — tap the pairs.
p: the teacher the poem speaks to
a tree that can fall at any time
how the Japji stanza is signed

s: the Oankar tells the pandit to throw away his books
it takes his letters and points them at the Name: listen, pandit, write the Name.
Guru Nanak signs a Japji stanza calling himself lowly
lowly Nanak offers this reflection, on ang four.

games.q: a learned teacher sits before you, proud of his letters. you have a song for him. how do you start?
o: prove him wrong in front of everyone.
invite him to listen, and use his own letters.
say nothing; learned people never change.
games.why: the Oankar's center line begins with listen, pandit, and the whole poem moves through the letters he already knows.

practice: Bring to mind something you know well, a recipe, a tool, a song, a line of scripture, and one person who might want to learn it.

Before planning what to say, remember the time you didn't know it, what confused you and what finally helped, and let your explanation start there, with one question you could ask them back. If you pray, say Waheguru once and rest.

wordCard.voice: Oankar close. Guru Nanak's alphabet poem, spoken to a teacher as an invitation: listen, write the Name. Humility for the learned, taught humbly. Today's word.

orig.note: paade: O pandit, O teacher; the word the Oankar's Rahao calls out to.

carryVoice: Your line: humble learning. The best teacher sits beside you. The Oankar, closed.
